title: Node.js
summary: The event loop, concurrency and how not to block the process.

cards.question: How does Node.js handle concurrency if it is single-threaded?
cards.answer: It runs your JavaScript on one thread and delegates I/O to libuv and the OS. When an operation finishes its callback is queued and the event loop runs it when the thread is free.

cards.question: In what order do process.nextTick, promises and setTimeout run?
cards.answer: process.nextTick and promise microtasks run when the current operation finishes, before returning to the event loop (nextTick first). setTimeout and setImmediate callbacks run later, in the timers and check phases.

cards.question: What happens if you do heavy computation in a handler?
cards.answer: It blocks the event loop: no other request is served until it finishes. Move CPU-bound work to worker_threads, a separate process or a job queue.

cards.question: What are streams and backpressure?
cards.answer: They process data in chunks instead of loading it all into memory. Backpressure is the signal a slow consumer uses to ask the producer to pause; pipeline() handles it and propagates errors.

cards.question: What is the difference between cluster and worker_threads?
cards.answer: cluster spawns independent processes sharing a port: it scales HTTP requests across cores. worker_threads spawns threads inside one process, with shareable memory, aimed at CPU-bound work.

cards.question: How do you gracefully shut down a Node.js service?
cards.answer: On SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, wait for in-flight requests to finish, close the database pool and exit with code 0, with a timeout in case something hangs.
